new-york.intro: New York City keeps an official register of its finest trees, the Parks Department's Great Trees of New York City, begun in 1985 and widened in 2024 after a public nomination drive drew more than 270 submissions. Most trees here carry that designation, and they stand in all five boroughs. On Staten Island they run from the Olmsted farmhouse to the shore below the Verrazzano; in northeast Queens, from the Queens Giant to the survivors of Flushing's old nurseries. A few earned their place another way, like a pear that came out of Ground Zero alive.
new-york.meta_description: New York keeps an official Great Trees register. Nearly seventy across all five boroughs, from a tulip tree older than the city to an Olmsted walnut.
new-york.question_meta: NYC's oldest tree is likely the Queens Giant, a 350-450 year old tulip tree in Alley Pond Park. Its story, location, and the city's other great trees.
new-york.question_answer: New York City's oldest tree is very likely the Queens Giant, a tulip tree in Alley Pond Park estimated between 350 and 450 years old by different measures, old enough to predate the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam entirely. It stands in a wooded section of the park in eastern Queens, reachable on foot from the Douglaston Long Island Rail Road station.
new-york.question_context: The Queens Giant's claim to being New York City's oldest living thing rests on measurement rather than legend. At 133.8 feet, it is the tallest carefully measured tree in the five boroughs, and tulip trees of that height in undisturbed forest are reliably centuries old; the New York City Parks Department states it is at least 368 years old, while some arborists place the range as wide as 350 to 450. Either figure puts its germination before the 1664 English takeover of New Amsterdam, and some local accounts connect trees in this stretch of Alley Pond Park to 17th century land dealings between the Dutch West India Company and the Matinecock people who lived here first, though no source ties this specific trunk to a documented transaction. What is not in question is that it has spent its entire life essentially unmanaged, growing in what is now protected forest rather than a planted garden, which is rare enough in New York that the Parks Department calls it possibly the oldest living organism in the metropolitan area. To get there, take the LIRR Port Washington line to Douglaston, then walk into Alley Pond Park's wooded trails.

faq_replace.Where is the best place to see old trees: No single spot has a monopoly. The Thain Family Forest at the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx is the largest surviving patch of the city's original woodland, but Central Park, Prospect Park, Kissena Park in Queens and a string of parks on Staten Island's shore each hold Great Trees of their own, and several of the best stand on ordinary sidewalks.
faq_replace.Are New York City's Great Trees free to: Most are. They stand in free public parks, cemeteries and on public sidewalks. The exceptions are the trees inside the New York Botanical Garden and Brooklyn Botanic Garden, which charge admission, and the catalpa inside Historic Richmond Town on Staten Island, a ticketed village. The Thain Family Forest tree at the Botanical Garden sits in woodland that is free to walk once you are inside the grounds.

faq_add.q: Where can I see several of New York's Great Trees on one walk?
faq_add.a: Prospect Park is the easiest. The Camperdown elm, a Japanese pagoda tree and an American hornbeam stand together south of the Boathouse, with a many-trunked English elm on the west drive. In Kissena Park, Queens, a Manchurian linden and a Persian ironwood from the old Parsons nursery stand about 90 metres apart, and in East Flatbush two black oaks believed to be left from Paerdegat Woods are a three-minute walk from each other.
